expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Applying SLD Exclusionary Criteria for an Emergent Bilingual
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A third grader who arrived from Guatemala 16 months ago tells detailed stories in Spanish but scores low on one English silent reading benchmark. Records show 24 absences during winter housing instability and a core reading curriculum lacking explicit phonics, yet a team member requests immediate SLD eligibility.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Apply IDEA SLD exclusionary criteria by assessing home-language literacy, instructional opportunity, and attendance before attributing difficulty to SLD.
expandableCase.explanation: IDEA prohibits identifying SLD when low achievement stems primarily from limited English proficiency, lack of appropriate reading instruction, or environmental disadvantage. Relying on one English benchmark without evaluating Spanish literacy and instructional quality conflates language difference with disability.

knowledgeChecks.prompt: When interpreting a student’s uneven learning profile, a kindergarten teacher notices that one child reaches several language milestones later than classmates. What is the most appropriate first interpretation?
choices: Broad developmental patterns allow wide variation, so the team should gather multi-source evidence across settings before drawing conclusions.
Falling below the typical classroom average on language milestones establishes a developmental disability that warrants formal eligibility.
The team should assign a provisional disability label promptly so specialized speech-language interventions can begin before gathering family input.
Chronological age norms become uninformative once a child trails classmates, so expectations should be based on informal adult impressions instead.
knowledgeChecks.rationale: Milestones provide useful reference points, not stand-alone diagnoses. Educators should document functioning across domains, contexts, and time and involve qualified team members before attributing a pattern to disability. For 5383 preparation, connect the response to the learner’s uneven skill profile, explicit and systematic instruction, appropriate access, culturally and linguistically responsive evidence, and observable progress rather than assuming that a learning-disability label predicts performance.

chapterTakeaways: Characterize SLD by an uneven intra-individual profile: intact reasoning or oral strengths alongside persistent, unexpected deficits in reading, writing, or mathematics despite instruction.
Distinguish second-language acquisition, dialect differences, and instructional gaps from intrinsic learning disabilities by examining home-language proficiency and prior opportunity to learn.
Recognize how executive functions (working memory, processing speed, cognitive flexibility, phonological processing) shape classroom performance across upper elementary and secondary grades.

expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Replacing Processing-Training Software with Targeted LD Instruction
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A fifth grader with SLD in reading fluency and coexisting ADHD struggles with multisyllabic decoding and multi-digit subtraction. Staff enroll him in a commercial auditory-processing brain-training app, assign generic LD worksheets, and blame his math errors solely on ADHD without analyzing conceptual gaps.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Replace unproven processing-training software with explicit decoding, fluency, and math instruction paired with targeted ADHD executive supports.
expandableCase.explanation: Empirical research shows isolated perceptual or cognitive processing training fails to generalize to reading or mathematics gains. Effective LD instruction directly remediates specific academic skill deficits while avoiding diagnostic overshadowing and one-size-fits-all worksheets that ignore individual profiles.

Deliver uniform remedial instruction across all core academic subjects so the student receives consistent skill reinforcement.
Interpret the persistent academic bottleneck as evidence of broadly limited cognitive ability across every learning domain.

Instruction should be based on the learner’s actual pattern of strengths and needs, not a global assumption. chapterTakeaways: Distinguish primary SLD subtypes: dyslexia (word-level decoding and spelling), dysgraphia (transcription and written expression), and dyscalculia (number sense and calculation).
Plan for frequent co-occurring conditions such as ADHD, developmental language disorder, anxiety, or low academic self-efficacy without letting secondary behavior mask core skill gaps.
Use error-pattern analysis rather than category labels to pinpoint whether reading breakdowns stem from phonemic decoding, orthographic fluency, vocabulary, or text-structure comprehension.

expandableCase.label: Applied SPED case
expandableCase.title: Aligning Measurable IEP Goals, Minutes, and Rigorous Access
expandableCase.clinicalDescription: A seventh grader with SLD in written expression has a draft IEP goal stating she will "improve paragraph writing with support," zero specialized writing minutes, and a copy-pasted list of 14 unused accommodations. Meanwhile, a teacher replaces grade-level history essays with third-grade coloring worksheets.
expandableCase.diagnosis: Write a measurable PLAAFP-linked writing goal with aligned specialized minutes and targeted accommodations that preserve grade-level curriculum rigor.
expandableCase.explanation: Under IDEA and the Endrew F. standard, annual goals must connect directly to objective baseline data with observable mastery criteria and matched specialized instruction. Boilerplate accommodation checklists obscure true needs, and lowering curriculum expectations unnecessarily denies access to grade-level general-education standards.

diagrams.title: SLD Profile, Coexisting-Needs Analysis & Dual-Need Instructional Alignment Flow

First, the educator builds a strength-based learner profile using diagnostic error-pattern analysis to identify concrete academic bottlenecks such as phonological processing deficits, orthographic decoding breakdowns, or working-memory constraints rather than making label-driven assumptions. Second, the team evaluates coexisting needs—including ADHD, academic anxiety, and sensory-environment triggers—so diagnostic overshadowing does not hide treatable attention or emotional barriers behind an SLD label. Third, teachers conduct a cognitive-load task breakdown, chunking multi-step directions, reducing extraneous visual or auditory clutter, and pairing explicit transition cues. Fourth, instruction combines evidence-based multisensory explicit academic routines with executive-function scaffolding and dual-need accommodations, rejecting generic remediation or unsupported cognitive processing-training fads. Finally, ongoing academic and engagement data verify whether both academic skill growth and coexisting self-regulation demands are improving, cycling back to error-pattern profiling when bottlenecks shift.

diagrams.title: PLAAFP-to-IEP Goal Architecture, Accommodations & Accessible Curriculum Flow
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Align objective PLAAFP baselines with standards-based measurable annual IEP goals (condition-behavior-criterion), distinguish accommodations from modifications, integrate UDL and Accessible Educational Materials (AEM), and review quarterly progress and transition alignment.

accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, the IEP team establishes objective PLAAFP baselines detailing measurable academic strengths, skill gaps, and how the learning disability affects involvement and progress in the general-education curriculum. Second, the team writes standards-aligned measurable annual IEP goals using a clear condition-behavior-criterion formula, avoiding vague objectives or goals disconnected from services. Third, the team differentiates accommodations—which preserve grade-level rigor while changing access, timing, setting, or response—from modifications that alter learning expectations, selecting individualized supplementary aids and Accessible Educational Materials (AEM) rather than boilerplate checklists. Fourth, teachers deliver UDL-aligned scaffolded instruction with leveled content-area text access and clear pacing bridges. Finally, teams conduct quarterly IEP progress reviews and secondary transition alignment, revising baselines, goals, or supplementary aids whenever growth stalls.

diagrams.title: Academic-Frustration FBA, Proactive BIP & Self-Regulation Support Cycle
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Interrupt the academic-frustration and task-escape cycle for learners with learning disabilities by pairing predictable routines and ABC functional assessment with proactive BIP replacement behaviors, metacognitive self-monitoring, and implementation fidelity checks.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow linking predictable classroom routines and ABC functional assessment to proactive BIP design, explicit self-regulation and help-seeking instruction, and fidelity-monitored reinforcement.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right behavioral support flow from predictable routines and ABC data through FBA functional hypothesis, proactive BIP and instructional scaffolding, and self-monitoring/help-seeking instruction to fidelity and PBIS outcome review.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, teachers establish predictable classroom routines and collect objective Antecedent-Behavior-Consequence (ABC) data when challenging behaviors arise during literacy, writing, or math tasks. Second, the team formulates an FBA functional hypothesis—often revealing an academic-frustration or task-escape function triggered by unaccommodated skill demands—rather than responding punitively to a skill deficit. Third, the team designs a proactive Behavior Intervention Plan (BIP) that modifies instructional antecedents, adds pre-teaching or chunked assignments, and prevents accidental escape reinforcement via premature task removal. Fourth, educators explicitly teach functionally equivalent replacement behaviors alongside metacognitive self-regulation strategies, including self-monitoring checklists, structured coping and help-seeking signals, and goal-setting with PBIS tiered reinforcement. Finally, the team conducts implementation fidelity checks and tracks behavior-plus-academic engagement data, returning to ABC observation whenever patterns persist.
textEquivalent: Predictable Routines & ABC Data Collection: Establish consistent classroom expectations and gather objective Antecedent-Behavior-Consequence observations during challenging academic tasks.
FBA Functional Hypothesis (Skill vs. Escape): Identify triggers and maintaining consequences—such as task-escape driven by academic frustration—rather than punishing underlying learning deficits.
Proactive BIP & Antecedent Scaffolds: Redesign triggering task demands with pre-teaching, chunked entry steps, and clear response rules that avoid accidental escape reinforcement.
Replacement Skills & Self-Regulation Routines: Explicitly teach help-seeking, coping scripts, self-monitoring checklists, and goal-setting reinforced through PBIS tiered feedback.
Fidelity Checks & Outcome Monitoring: Verify consistent staff execution of the BIP and track both behavioral reduction and academic task engagement, refining the FBA if behavior persists.

diagrams.title: Executive Function, Strategy Instruction & Assistive Technology Access Loop
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Align executive-function strategy routines, feature-matched assistive technology, and rigor-preserving accommodations so learners with learning disabilities access grade-level content without lowering academic expectations.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow showing how identifying executive-function and mechanics barriers drives explicit study routines, matched assistive technology, rigor-preserving accommodations, and self-advocacy monitoring.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right access loop from pinpointing executive-function and mechanics barriers through explicit study routines, feature-matched AT tools, and rigor-preserving accommodations to usage monitoring and self-advocacy.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, the team identifies specific executive-function and access barriers—such as working-memory overload, task initiation, organization, decoding fatigue, or handwriting bottlenecks—matched to classroom environments and tasks. Second, educators explicitly teach metacognitive and study routines including chunking, planner workflows, structured note-taking frames, and self-monitoring checklists. Third, the team matches assistive technology tools—such as text-to-speech, audiobooks, speech-to-text dictation, word prediction, and digital graphic organizers—paired with direct training on tool use. Fourth, aligned instructional and testing accommodations preserve grade-level cognitive rigor while removing construct-irrelevant mechanics barriers. Finally, educators monitor AT usage and student independence while coaching self-advocacy, looping back to re-evaluate task demands and feature fit as grade-level complexity increases.

Explicit Study & Metacognitive Routines: Directly teach and rehearse task chunking, visual checklists, note-taking frames, time-estimation scripts, and self-monitoring cues rather than assuming independent study habits.

Feature-Matched Assistive Technology Tools: Match text-to-speech, speech-to-text, word prediction, audiobooks, and digital graphic organizers to student needs and provide structured training in how to use them effectively.

Rigor-Preserving Accommodations: Deliver IEP-documented classroom and testing accommodations that eliminate construct-irrelevant barriers while preserving grade-level academic standards and avoiding unnecessary modifications.

Usage Monitoring & Learner Self-Advocacy: Track whether routines and AT genuinely increase independence and output quality, coaching students to self-advocate and looping back to refine tools as coursework demands evolve.

diagrams.title: Structured Literacy & Evidence-Based Reading Intervention Sequence
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Sequence evidence-based reading intervention for students with learning disabilities from diagnostic skill pinpointing through explicit phonemic, phonics, and morphological instruction, guided fluency and vocabulary scaffolds, comprehension strategy instruction, and connected-text transfer.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow linking diagnostic reading pinpointing to explicit word-level instruction, fluency and vocabulary scaffolds, comprehension strategies, and authentic connected-text transfer.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right reading intervention flow from diagnostic skill pinpointing through explicit phonics/morphology, guided fluency and vocabulary, and comprehension strategies to connected-text transfer.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, the teacher conducts diagnostic reading assessment to pinpoint whether breakdowns stem from phonemic awareness, phonics and syllable decoding, multisyllabic morphology, oral reading fluency, academic vocabulary, or language comprehension. Second, explicit, systematic, cumulative structured literacy instruction directly teaches phoneme-grapheme correspondences, syllable types, prefixes, suffixes, and roots with immediate corrective feedback. Third, guided fluency and vocabulary scaffolds pair modeled prosody, repeated or partner reading, and explicit morphological vocabulary routines to build automaticity and word knowledge. Fourth, comprehension strategy instruction explicitly models text-structure mapping, summarizing, self-questioning, and comprehension monitoring using think-alouds and graphic organizers. Finally, learners transfer skills into connected narrative and informational texts across general-education classes, with ongoing error analysis cycling back to diagnostic pinpointing whenever word-level or comprehension bottlenecks persist.
textEquivalent: Diagnostic Skill Pinpointing: Use screening and diagnostic probes to isolate specific breakdowns across phonemic awareness, decoding, multisyllabic morphology, reading fluency, vocabulary, or text comprehension.

Explicit Phonemic, Phonics & Morphological Instruction: Deliver cumulative, systematic instruction in phoneme-grapheme correspondences, six syllable types, spelling patterns, and morphemes (roots, prefixes, suffixes) with immediate corrective feedback.

Guided Fluency & Vocabulary Scaffolds: Build automaticity and prosody through repeated reading, choral/partner reading, and decodable-to-authentic text bridging paired with direct academic vocabulary instruction.
Comprehension Strategy Instruction: Explicitly teach text structures, gist summarizing, self-questioning, and inference monitoring via teacher think-alouds and structured visual organizers.
Connected-Text Transfer & Monitoring: Fade scaffolds into grade-level connected texts across content subjects, re-pinpointing decoding or language gaps whenever accuracy or comprehension dips.

diagrams.title: Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD) & Written Expression Scaffold Flow
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Guide learners with written-expression disabilities through the Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD) stages—building background knowledge, teacher think-aloud modeling, mnemonic memorization and graphic-organizer support, and independent planning, drafting, and revision.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow illustrating the mastery-based SRSD sequence for written expression from background knowledge and think-aloud modeling through supported organizers to independent drafting and revision.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right SRSD writing flow from developing background knowledge and strategy discussion through teacher think-aloud modeling, memorization with graphic organizers, and independent drafting to structured revision.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, the teacher develops prerequisite genre background knowledge, spelling and sentence-combining skills, and discusses how a mnemonic strategy (such as POW+TREE for opinion essays or STOP+DARE for persuasive writing) improves writing quality. Second, the teacher conducts explicit think-aloud modeling, composing aloud while demonstrating planning, self-talk statements, coping with frustration, and self-monitoring. Third, students memorize the strategy steps and receive scaffolded support using graphic organizers, sentence frames, and self-graphing of essay elements until mastery criteria are met. Fourth, scaffolds fade so learners independently plan, organize, and draft coherent paragraphs while applying self-monitoring cues. Finally, students execute structured revision and editing routines—checking ideas, organization, transitions, and conventions—and generalize the strategy across content areas, cycling back to organizer scaffolds whenever an unfamiliar writing genre is introduced.
textEquivalent: Develop Background Knowledge & Discuss Strategy: Build genre concepts, vocabulary, and sentence prerequisites while examining strong models and gaining student buy-in for an explicit writing mnemonic (e.g., POW+TREE).
Teacher Think-Aloud Modeling: Model the entire writing process aloud, showing how to generate ideas, organize notes, use encouraging self-talk statements, and monitor progress in real time.

Memorize Mnemonic & Graphic-Organizer Support: Practice strategy steps to automaticity and co-write using graphic organizers, sentence-combining frames, and self-graphing charts until mastery is consistent.

Independent Planning, Drafting & Self-Monitoring: Fade external cue cards as learners independently plan notes, compose cohesive drafts, and verify all required genre elements using internalized self-regulation.
Structured Revision & Genre Generalization: Apply explicit revision and editing checklists for clarity, evidence, and mechanics, transferring the SRSD routine across ELA, science, and social studies.

diagrams.title: Mathematics Intervention Sequence: CRA Progression & Schema-Based Problem Solving
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Connect conceptual understanding to procedural fluency and word-problem transfer using the Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA) sequence, number-line models, worked examples, and schema-based problem solving.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow advancing math intervention from concrete manipulatives and number lines through semi-concrete visuals and abstract fluency to schema-based word-problem transfer.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right mathematics intervention flow from concrete manipulatives and number lines through semi-concrete visuals, abstract algorithms and fact fluency, and schema-based problem solving to multi-step transfer.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, learners build conceptual grounding using concrete manipulatives—such as base-ten blocks, fraction tiles, algebra tiles, and physical number lines—paired with precise mathematical language. Second, semi-concrete visual representations (strip or tape diagrams, area models, drawn arrays, and open number lines) bridge physical actions directly to mathematical symbols. Third, explicit instruction links visual models to abstract algorithms, worked examples, and brief cumulative retrieval practice to establish strategic fact and computational fluency. Fourth, schema-based instruction teaches students to recognize underlying additive schemas (total, difference, change) and multiplicative schemas (equal groups, comparison, ratios) rather than relying on unreliable keyword tricks. Finally, learners transfer schemas to multi-step contextual problems and verify reasonableness via estimation, stepping back to visual strip diagrams or number lines whenever problem structure breaks down.
textEquivalent: Concrete Manipulatives & Number-Line Models: Build deep number sense, place value, and fraction magnitude with tactile base-ten blocks, fraction strips, algebra tiles, and physical number lines paired with precise mathematical vocabulary.

Semi-Concrete Visual Representations: Transition from physical objects to strip diagrams, area models, open number lines, and arrays while writing parallel symbolic equations to maintain explicit connections.
Abstract Algorithms & Fact Fluency: Connect visual understanding to efficient symbolic procedures, annotated worked examples, and brief cumulative retrieval practice for foundational math facts.

Schema-Based Word-Problem Solving: Explicitly teach underlying mathematical structures—additive (total, difference, change) and multiplicative (equal groups, comparison, ratios)—replacing brittle keyword shortcuts.

Multi-Step Transfer & Reasonableness Check: Apply problem schemas to unfamiliar multi-step tasks, estimate answers on number lines to verify reasonableness, and return to visual models when conceptual errors surface.

diagrams.title: Specific Learning Disability (SLD) Identification & Exclusionary-Factors Decision Flow
diagrams.learnerPurpose: Apply IDEA SLD eligibility criteria by systematically ruling out exclusionary factors, integrating RTI/MTSS response data with a nondiscriminatory multidisciplinary evaluation, confirming an SLD profile across reading, writing, or math, and linking findings to IEP eligibility and PLAAFP.
diagrams.caption: An original study flow tracing IDEA SLD identification from exclusionary-factor screening and RTI/MTSS response data through comprehensive evaluation, SLD profile synthesis, and IEP PLAAFP initiation.

accessibility.shortAlt: Left-to-right flow from exclusionary-factor rule-outs through RTI/MTSS response data, comprehensive multidisciplinary evaluation, and SLD profile synthesis to IEP eligibility and PLAAFP.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, the evaluation team rules out IDEA exclusionary factors under 34 CFR 300.309—confirming that underachievement is not primarily the result of visual, hearing, or motor disabilities, intellectual disability, emotional disturbance, cultural or economic disadvantage, lack of appropriate reading or math instruction, or limited English proficiency. Second, the team reviews documented RTI/MTSS instruction fidelity and repeated progress-monitoring response data without using tiered intervention to delay or deny an evaluation. Third, qualified professionals conduct a nondiscriminatory, multi-source comprehensive evaluation including classroom observation, standardized and curriculum-based academic measures, language dominance checks, and caregiver input. Fourth, the team synthesizes convergent data to identify an SLD profile across oral expression, listening comprehension, written expression, basic reading, reading fluency, reading comprehension, mathematics calculation, or mathematics problem solving requiring specially designed instruction; if exclusionary factors explain the need, the student returns to targeted Tier 2/3 MTSS or language supports. Finally, eligible learners move within 30 calendar days to IEP development grounded in objective PLAAFP baselines.
textEquivalent: Exclusionary-Factors Rule-Out Screen: Confirm underachievement is not primarily caused by visual, hearing, or motor disabilities, intellectual disability, emotional disturbance, cultural/environmental/economic disadvantage, lack of appropriate reading or math instruction, or limited English proficiency (34 CFR 300.309).

RTI/MTSS Response & Fidelity Data: Document delivery of evidence-based instruction with fidelity and repeated progress-monitoring measures of student response, ensuring MTSS never delays or denies a warranted or parent-requested initial evaluation.

Comprehensive Multidisciplinary Evaluation: Gather nondiscriminatory, multi-source evidence across all suspected areas—including required classroom observation, academic achievement testing, linguistic/cultural context, and parent/teacher input—without relying on any single measure.

SLD Profile & Adverse-Impact Synthesis: Verify inadequate achievement relative to grade-level standards across specific reading, writing, math, or oral-language domains plus adverse educational impact requiring specially designed instruction.

accessibility.shortAlt: Top-to-bottom legal compliance workflow from Child Find and Section 504 duty through Prior Written Notice and informed consent, collaborative FAPE/LRE and equitable accommodations, and MDR disciplinary safeguards to FERPA confidentiality and dispute prevention.
accessibility.longDescription: Read from top to bottom. First, districts fulfill their affirmative IDEA Child Find duty and Section 504 nondiscrimination mandate, ensuring informal classroom help never substitutes for or delays referral when a disability is suspected. Second, teams issue Prior Written Notice (PWN) in understandable native language and obtain informed written parental consent before initial evaluation or initial special-education services, providing full procedural safeguards notices. Third, the full IEP team makes collaborative FAPE, LRE placement, and equitable testing-accommodation decisions without unilateral changes or predetermination. Fourth, whenever disciplinary removals exceed 10 school days or create a pattern of removal, the team conducts a Manifestation Determination Review (MDR) to determine whether conduct was directly related to the disability or a failure to implement the IEP. Finally, educators uphold FERPA confidentiality across all IEP records and assessment data while building transparent family communication and student self-advocacy to prevent due-process disputes.
textEquivalent: Child Find & Section 504 Affirmative Duty: Actively identify, locate, and evaluate students suspected of needing IDEA special education or Section 504 accommodations without using informal help to delay referral.

Prior Written Notice & Informed Consent: Deliver clear Prior Written Notice (PWN) and procedural safeguards in the family native language and secure informed written consent before initial evaluation or services.

Collaborative FAPE, LRE & Testing Equity: Determine IEP services, Least Restrictive Environment placement, and equitable testing accommodations collaboratively—never via predetermination or unilateral changes.

Manifestation Determination Review (MDR): Convene an MDR within 10 school days of a disciplinary change of placement to evaluate disability nexus and IEP implementation fidelity before exclusionary action.

FERPA Confidentiality & Dispute Prevention: Restrict IEP and evaluation records to staff with legitimate educational interest, document decisions transparently, and support student self-advocacy rights.

diagrams.learnerPurpose: Integrate validated weekly Curriculum-Based Measurement (CBM) probes, aim-line decision rules, and Data-Based Individualization (DBI) intensification with general-education co-teaching, family partnership, and transition self-advocacy.

accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, educators administer brief, validated weekly Curriculum-Based Measurement (CBM) probes in reading, writing, or mathematics using alternate equivalent forms aligned to annual IEP goals. Second, graphed scores are compared against the student’s aim line using objective decision rules—such as the 4-point rule where four consecutive scores below the aim line trigger an instructional change and four consecutive scores above warrant raising the goal. Third, when response is insufficient, Data-Based Individualization (DBI) intensifies instruction by adjusting dosage, group size, explicitness, feedback immediacy, or diagnostic skill focus rather than repeating an ineffective routine. Fourth, special and general educators coordinate purposeful co-teaching models (station, parallel, alternative, or team teaching) so intensified SDI aligns seamlessly with grade-level content. Finally, the team shares transparent progress graphs with families and coaches student transition self-advocacy, looping continuously back into weekly CBM monitoring.

diagrams.learnerPurpose: Sustain high-integrity special education practice for students with learning disabilities by upholding CEC ethical and scope-of-competence boundaries, auditing intervention fidelity, vetting evidence-based practices, documenting paraprofessional supervision, and advancing systemic equity and student self-advocacy.

accessibility.longDescription: Read from left to right. First, special educators anchor every decision in Council for Exceptional Children (CEC) ethical standards and strict scope-of-competence boundaries—collaborating with school psychologists, SLPs, and medical professionals rather than making clinical diagnoses outside licensure. Second, teachers conduct data-driven instructional reflection and intervention fidelity self-audits before altering instructional variables without evidence. Third, educators vet instructional programs against peer-reviewed evidence-based practice standards and engage in needs-aligned professional learning communities (PLCs) and instructional coaching, rejecting unvalidated commercial fads. Fourth, teachers provide clear written routines, modeled coaching, and supervision logs for paraprofessionals supporting students with learning disabilities. Finally, educators advance systemic equity and student-led transition self-advocacy, feeding student outcome evidence back into ongoing ethical reflection and professional learning priorities.

EBP Vetting & Targeted PLC Coaching: Evaluate programs against rigorous research evidence to reject unvalidated commercial fads, pursuing coaching and PLCs aligned to student needs.

Paraprofessional Training & Supervision Logs: Direct paraprofessionals with written instructional protocols, modeled feedback, and documented supervision while retaining teacher responsibility for SDI.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: SLD IDEA exclusionary criteria & RTI/PSW evaluation
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Audit Exclusionary Factors and RTI Dosage Before Making an SLD Eligibility Call
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Evaluate a fourth-grade referral packet containing conflicting RTI slopes, cognitive processing subtests, and attendance records to determine what evidence is required under IDEA 34 CFR 300.309 before deciding SLD eligibility.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Caleb (Grade 4) reads 52 words correct per minute on grade-level passages (benchmark 105) with a 0.5-word weekly slope across eight Tier 2 weeks. Records show he transferred schools twice in Grade 2, missed 19 school days this year, and had a substitute teacher during 6 of 8 Tier 2 weeks with no fidelity logs. On psychological testing, his verbal comprehension is 104, phonological processing is 76, and oral science discussions are strong.
taskParts: Analyze how Caleb's school mobility, 19 absences, and unverified Tier 2 substitute instruction affect IDEA 34 CFR 300.309 exclusionary criteria regarding lack of appropriate instruction in reading.

Explain how a multidisciplinary team should integrate RTI progress-monitoring data, pattern of strengths and weaknesses (PSW) findings, and mandatory classroom observation without relying on a single score or IQ-achievement discrepancy.
Specify the immediate data-verification steps, parent-communication safeguards, and instructional supports required while completing a compliant SLD eligibility determination.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Weigh Caleb's 52 WRCM score, flat 0.5 weekly slope, and 76 phonological processing score against his 104 verbal comprehension, strong oral science reasoning, 19 absences, and 6 undocumented substitute-led Tier 2 weeks.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply 34 CFR 300.309 rules requiring documentation of appropriate reading instruction by qualified personnel, repeated achievement assessments, classroom observation, and ruling out primary exclusionary factors before confirming SLD.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Deliver high-fidelity, explicit phonological and decoding intervention with trained staff, conduct a structured general-education reading observation, and collect family developmental and attendance-barrier history.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Protect IDEA evaluation timelines without using unverified RTI to delay parental consent, document intervention fidelity checklists weekly, and provide parents clear written notice of every data source reviewed.

successCriteria: Explicitly flags the 6 undocumented substitute-led Tier 2 weeks and 19 absences as threats to proving Caleb received appropriate reading instruction under 34 CFR 300.309(b).
Integrates Caleb's 104 verbal comprehension and 76 phonological processing pattern with classroom work samples and direct observation rather than treating any single subtest as definitive.
Identifies the mandatory IDEA classroom observation in Caleb's area of reading difficulty and collaboration with parents to address attendance barriers.
Maintains strict adherence to IDEA evaluation timelines while immediately restoring fidelity-monitored, explicit reading instruction.
commonPitfalls: Declaring Caleb SLD solely because of the 28-point spread between verbal comprehension (104) and phonological processing (76) without validating instructional opportunity.
Automatically denying SLD eligibility because Caleb missed 19 days rather than investigating whether his severe phonological deficit persists during verified high-fidelity instruction.
Treating undocumented substitute-led sessions as proof of nonresponse to evidence-based Tier 2 intervention.
Omitting the required general-education classroom observation and repeated progress-monitoring documentation mandated by 34 CFR 300.309 and 300.310.
sampleOutline: Instructional-opportunity audit: Six substitute-led Tier 2 weeks without fidelity logs plus 19 absences prevent the team from claiming Caleb failed to respond to verified reading instruction.

Converging evaluation synthesis: Pair Caleb's 76 phonological score and 52 WRCM baseline with a structured classroom reading observation, phonics error inventory, and parent interview on early language and attendance.

IDEA 300.309 decision framework: Rule out visual, hearing, motor, emotional, environmental, and instructional-opportunity explanations while documenting whether phonological deficits persist despite qualified explicit teaching.

Concurrent action and safeguards: Honor the statutory evaluation clock, share repeated CBM graphs with parents, partner to resolve absences, and immediately restore fidelity-checked structured literacy sessions.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: Explicit phonological, orthographic & morphological reading SDI
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Design Multisyllabic Decoding and Morphology SDI for an Upper-Elementary Reader
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Use diagnostic word-reading, spelling, and oral reading error data for a fifth-grade student with dyslexia to build an explicit structured-literacy Specially Designed Instruction (SDI) sequence that transfers to connected Grade 5 text.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Tessa (Grade 5, SLD in basic reading skills and fluency) reads single-syllable CVC and silent-e words at 95% accuracy but drops to 58% on multisyllabic words in Grade 5 social studies text. Miscue analysis shows she guesses from initial letters ("conclude" as "collect", "transportation" as "transparent"), omits medial vowel teams, and spells "unbelievable" as "unbelevbl." Her oral listening comprehension is at the 78th percentile.
taskParts: Interpret Tessa's miscue and spelling profile to pinpoint the exact phonological, syllable-division, orthographic, and morphological gaps driving her 58% multisyllabic accuracy.

Design a systematic, explicit SDI lesson sequence (modeling, guided practice, corrective feedback, and cumulative review) targeting multisyllabic word-attack routines and high-utility prefixes, roots, and suffixes.
Specify how to bridge isolated word study into Grade 5 fluency and comprehension while monitoring orthographic transfer weekly.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Connect Tessa's 95% single-syllable mastery and 78th-percentile listening comprehension against her 58% multisyllabic accuracy, initial-letter guessing, medial vowel omissions, and spelling of "unbelevbl."

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply WWC Grades 4-9 reading intervention recommendations: teach explicit multisyllabic decoding routines, morphological analysis (affixes and roots), and structured connected-text fluency practice.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Implement a daily 4-step word-attack routine (circle prefixes/suffixes, underline vowel graphemes, divide and flex syllables, blend and check meaning) paired with encoding dictation and partner repeated reading.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Collect weekly multisyllabic nonsense-and-real-word probes, dictated morphological spelling checks, and oral reading accuracy/rate graphs while preserving Tessa's access to Grade 5 concepts via audio.

successCriteria: Accurately diagnoses Tessa's reliance on initial-letter guessing and weak medial-vowel/morpheme mapping despite intact single-syllable decoding and strong listening comprehension.
Constructs an explicit, systematic SDI sequence (I do, we do, you do) teaching both syllable-division strategies and structural/morphological analysis rather than whole-word memorization.
Integrates encoding (spelling dictation) and connected Grade 5 text practice so decoded words transfer to authentic fluency and comprehension.
Establishes weekly diagnostic mastery criteria and protects Tessa's access to Grade 5 social studies knowledge through text-to-speech while remediation proceeds.
commonPitfalls: Encouraging Tessa to guess multisyllabic words using picture clues or surrounding sentence context (three-cueing), which reinforces her initial-letter guessing habit.
Re-teaching kindergarten CVC phonics drills even though Tessa already decodes single-syllable closed and silent-e words at 95% accuracy.
Having Tessa copy weekly vocabulary lists five times each without explicit phoneme-grapheme or morpheme mapping.
Pulling Tessa into simplified Grade 2 reading comprehension books that starve her 78th-percentile oral language and background knowledge.
sampleOutline: Diagnostic profile: Tessa's 95% single-syllable mastery and 78th-percentile listening comprehension rule out broad language deficits; her core breakdown is multisyllabic vowel mapping and morphological segmentation.

Explicit decoding and morphology SDI: Explicitly model peeling high-frequency prefixes and suffixes (un-, trans-, -port-, -able), locating vowel teams per syllable, and flexing schwa pronunciations with immediate corrective feedback.

Encoding and text transfer: Pair decoded word families with morpheme-by-morpheme spelling dictation, then practice targeted Grade 5 social studies paragraphs through choral and timed partner rereading.
Progress monitoring: Track weekly accuracy on unpracticed multisyllabic words and connected-text WCPM while providing audio access to full Grade 5 textbooks so content learning never stalls.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: CRA & schema-based math SDI with CBM decision rules
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Repair Multiplicative Word-Problem Errors Using CRA, Schemas, and CBM Rules
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Analyze a fourth-grade student's mathematics error patterns and flat CBM graph to redesign Specially Designed Instruction using Concrete-Representational-Abstract (CRA) progression, schema-based instruction, and explicit data-decision rules.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Malik (Grade 4, SLD in math calculation and problem solving) adds every number when he sees "more" or "altogether," scoring 25% on multiplicative comparison items. He writes 1/4 is larger than 1/2 because 4 is bigger than 2. Weekly math-concepts CBM probes show four straight scores below his aimline (8, 9, 8, 9 vs. aimline 14). Current support relies on keyword posters and flash-card drills.
taskParts: Diagnose the conceptual misconceptions behind Malik's keyword guessing and whole-number bias in fractions, and explain why four consecutive CBM points below the aimline mandate an instructional change.
Design an explicit CRA and schema-based SDI sequence targeting multiplicative comparison word problems and fraction magnitude on number lines.
Define clear CBM progress-monitoring procedures, error-analysis checks, and four-point decision rules to evaluate whether the revised math SDI accelerates Malik's slope.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Pair Malik's 25% multiplicative comparison score, keyword-triggered addition errors, whole-number fraction misconception (1/4 over 1/2), and four consecutive CBM points stuck at 8-9 against a 14-point aimline.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply WWC elementary math intervention recommendations: replace keyword tricks with schema-based problem solving, use CRA visual representations including number lines, and apply data-based individualization.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Remove keyword posters; model equal-groups and multiplicative comparison tape diagrams with manipulatives before symbolic equations, and teach fraction magnitude using concrete strips aligned to 0-to-1 number lines.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Graph weekly parallel math CBM probes against the IEP aimline, run error-pattern checks every two weeks, and trigger a documented DBI intensification if four consecutive scores remain below the aimline.

successCriteria: Explicitly rejects keyword-poster instruction as counterproductive and identifies whole-number bias in Malik's fraction comparison error.
Applies the four-point CBM decision rule (four consecutive data points below the aimline) to justify an immediate instructional redesign rather than waiting for the annual IEP review.
Sequences explicit CRA instruction (concrete manipulatives to tape diagrams/number lines to abstract equations) alongside schema-based problem classification.
Incorporates brief daily fluency practice paired with conceptual feedback and clear fidelity plus biweekly error-pattern reviews.
commonPitfalls: Doubling the number of multiplication flash-card drills while leaving Malik's conceptual schema and fraction-magnitude gaps unaddressed.
Teaching expanded "keyword cheat sheets" (such as circling "more" to add or "times" to multiply), which fails on multi-step and comparison problems.
Waiting until the end of the grading quarter to adjust SDI even though four consecutive weekly CBM probes sit flat below the aimline.
Skipping directly from concrete fraction tiles to cross-multiplication rules without linking pictorial number lines to abstract symbols.
sampleOutline: Error and CBM diagnosis: Four straight CBM scores of 8-9 against an aimline of 14 trigger an immediate DBI change; Malik's errors reflect keyword dependency and whole-number fraction bias rather than mere fact-recall slowness.

Schema-based problem solving: Replace keyword posters with explicit attack strategies (read, identify problem schema, draw a multiplicative comparison bar model, write equation, verify reasonableness).

CRA fraction-magnitude sequence: Move systematically from concrete fraction bars to partitioned number lines to symbolic inequality comparisons so Malik sees why larger denominators create smaller unit parts.

CBM decision protocol: Maintain weekly comparable probes, insert a vertical phase-change line on the graph, audit instructional fidelity, and reconvene the IEP team if the new slope still lags after four to six weeks.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: SRSD writing SDI & executive-function assistive technology
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Combine SRSD Argument Writing with Speech-to-Text and Executive-Function Supports
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Plan Specially Designed Instruction and assistive technology integration for a seventh-grade student with dysgraphia and working-memory challenges so she can independently plan, draft, and revise Grade 7 argumentative essays.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Hannah (Grade 7, SLD in written expression with dysgraphia and slow orthographic motor speed) speaks clearly during debate and cites two text sources accurately aloud. When handwriting a 25-minute essay, she produces only 38 cramped words with omitted endings, no counterargument, and frequent off-topic restarts. Her current IEP lists only "extended time" and "copies of teacher notes," and teachers occasionally excuse her from essays altogether.
taskParts: Analyze how Hannah's oral debate strengths versus her 38-word handwritten output separate transcription/executive-function barriers from higher-order argumentative reasoning.
Design a six-stage Self-Regulated Strategy Development (SRSD) writing plan (such as POW+TREE or STOP+DARE) incorporating explicit self-talk, goal setting, and revision checklists.
Select and justify matched assistive technology (speech-to-text, word prediction, text-to-speech playback for editing) alongside a training and fading routine that ends essay exemptions.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Contrast Hannah's accurate oral source citations during debate against her 38-word handwritten draft, omitted endings, missing counterargument, and ineffective accommodations that led to essay exemptions.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply evidence-based SRSD writing stages, IDEA assistive technology consideration and service training duties, and WWC adolescent literacy guidance integrating explicit writing-strategy instruction with reading.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Teach an explicit argumentative SRSD mnemonic with graphic planners and self-monitoring checklists while training Hannah to dictate drafts via speech-to-text and revise using text-to-speech read-back.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Score biweekly argumentative essays with an analytic rubric (claim, evidence, counterargument, transitions, conventions) and track independent AT workflow fluency across ELA and social studies.

successCriteria: Distinguishes transcription/working-memory overload from conceptual knowledge and explicitly rejects excusing Hannah from grade-level essays.

Details concrete SRSD stages (develop background knowledge, discuss, model with think-alouds, memorize mnemonic, support with scaffolds, independent performance) rather than handing out an untaught organizer.
Pairs speech-to-text and word prediction with explicit instruction in punctuation dictation and text-to-speech auditory proofreading so AT builds rather than replaces writing skill.
Establishes objective rubric and word-production/essay-element progress monitoring across multiple content classes.
commonPitfalls: Continuing to excuse Hannah from written arguments or substituting fill-in-the-blank worksheets, which lowers Grade 7 academic expectations.
Turning on speech-to-text without explicitly teaching planning, spoken punctuation commands, and text-to-speech editing routines.
Relying solely on extended time, which prolongs motor fatigue without reducing dysgraphia transcription bottlenecks.
Grading only spelling mechanics while ignoring Hannah's mastery of claim, textual evidence, and counterargument organization.
sampleOutline: Profile synthesis: Hannah's strong oral debate citations prove she understands argumentative reasoning; her 38-word drafts reflect severe transcription load and unguided planning rather than weak content knowledge.

SRSD instructional cycle: Explicitly model POW+TREE (or STOP+DARE) using think-alouds, co-construct argument organizers, embed self-regulation checklists, and gradually fade visual prompts toward independence.

Integrated AT workflow: Conduct a feature-matched trial of speech-to-text plus word prediction for drafting and text-to-speech read-back for auditory editing, writing both AT devices and staff/student training into the IEP.

Generalization and monitoring: End essay exemptions across core classes, measure essay elements and total words written biweekly via analytic rubrics, and align daily AT supports with allowable state testing accommodations.

constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Interrupt Escape-Maintained Reading Avoidance with Academic Antecedents and Self-Regulation
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Interpret functional behavior assessment data for a sixth-grade student with SLD whose disruptive outbursts occur exclusively during independent reading and math problem sets, and design an integrated academic-behavioral intervention plan.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Diego (Grade 6, SLD in reading fluency and math reasoning) throws his binder, makes sarcastic jokes, or walks to the nurse during silent reading and word-problem blocks. Over 12 observation days, 14 of 16 incidents occurred within 4 minutes of dense multi-paragraph handouts and ended with a 15-minute hallway cool-down or nurse visit. During hands-on science labs and audio-supported discussions, he had zero incidents and completed 90% of tasks.
taskParts: Construct a clear ABC functional hypothesis linking Diego's academic skill barriers to the negative reinforcement cycle maintaining his disruptive behavior.

Design a proactive BIP that pairs antecedent academic access supports (text chunking, audio/preview scaffolds, worked examples) with explicit teaching of a dignified self-advocacy replacement skill and self-monitoring.
Specify how teachers will avoid reinforcing task escape during incidents while tracking both replacement-skill usage and independent academic completion.

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Contrast the 14 of 16 incidents occurring within 4 minutes of dense handouts (ending in 15-minute nurse/hallway escapes) against Diego's zero incidents and 90% completion during audio-supported labs.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply functional behavioral assessment logic, negative reinforcement mechanics, explicit adolescent reading/math scaffolding, and self-regulation strategy instruction without punitive exclusion.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Pre-teach key vocabulary, chunk dense handouts with audio/worked-model access, teach a discreet help-or-two-minute-reset pass, and coach Diego to self-graph task starts and check-ins.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Collect daily latency to task initiation, percentage of chunked work completed, discreet pass frequency, and office/nurse exit counts while checking adult fidelity to non-punitive redirection.

successCriteria: Correctly identifies escape from aversive reading/math task demands (rather than peer attention alone) as the primary hypothesized behavioral function.

Addresses the root academic trigger through antecedent SDI and access scaffolds (chunked passages, vocabulary preview, worked examples, audio support) instead of relying solely on behavioral contingencies.
Teaches a socially dignified, age-appropriate middle-school replacement behavior (discreet check-in cue or brief structured reset with immediate return to scaffolded work).
Includes explicit self-monitoring goals and fidelity checks so staff stop inadvertently reinforcing task avoidance with 15-minute hallway or nurse removals.
commonPitfalls: Diagnosing Diego's sarcastic jokes as pure attention-seeking without noticing that 87.5% of incidents begin with dense text and end in task removal.
Assigning detention or in-school suspension for binder-throwing, which escalates academic frustration and still allows Diego to escape the assignment.
Using an embarrassing elementary sticker chart in front of sixth-grade peers instead of a private self-monitoring card and natural reinforcers.
Allowing open-ended nurse visits whenever Diego requests a break instead of pairing a brief structured reset with scaffolded task completion.
sampleOutline: Functional hypothesis: Dense, unscaffolded multi-paragraph reading and word-problem handouts trigger academic embarrassment and frustration; binder-throwing and jokes are negatively reinforced by 15-minute hallway or nurse escapes.
Antecedent academic repairs: Provide digital audio access, pre-taught academic vocabulary, worked math examples, and chunked two-part checkpoints before independent work begins.

Replacement and self-regulation teaching: Privately rehearse a discreet desk signal for immediate teacher check-in or a timed 2-minute reset, paired with a private self-monitoring tracker for task initiation.

Consequence shift and data review: Prompt the taught help signal at early frustration cues, maintain brief instructional follow-through rather than lengthy removals, and review weekly work completion alongside incident counts.

constructedResponseWorkshops.taskType: IDEA procedural safeguards & secondary self-advocacy transition
constructedResponseWorkshops.title: Build a Compliant Secondary Transition Plan and Self-Advocacy Bridge to College
constructedResponseWorkshops.prompt: Audit a tenth-grade transition IEP for a student with SLD who plans to enter a community-college nursing-assistant program, correcting procedural safeguard omissions and strengthening measurable postsecondary goals and self-advocacy instruction.
constructedResponseWorkshops.stimulus: Aaliyah (Grade 10, age 16, SLD in reading comprehension and math fluency) wants to earn a CNA certificate and an associate nursing degree. Her draft IEP was written without inviting Aaliyah or giving a transition assessment; it states only "Aaliyah will graduate and go to college." She cannot explain her disability or needs because teachers always arrange her extended time and audio texts automatically.
taskParts: Identify the IDEA secondary transition and procedural-safeguard violations in Aaliyah's draft IEP, including missing student invitation, age-appropriate transition assessments, and non-measurable postsecondary goals.
Draft aligned, measurable postsecondary goals (education/training and employment), coordinated transition services, and an annual IEP self-advocacy goal grounded in her nursing pathway.
Explain how to prepare Aaliyah for the legal shift from IDEA K-12 entitlements to ADA/Section 504 college disability services, including documentation readiness and the Summary of Performance (SOP).

planningFrame.label: Evidence
planningFrame.guidance: Anchor revisions in Aaliyah's age (16), nursing-assistant and associate-degree career goals, reading comprehension and math fluency profile, omitted transition assessment, and passive reliance on teacher-initiated accommodations.

planningFrame.label: IDEA & EBP rule
planningFrame.guidance: Apply IDEA transition mandates effective by age 16 (student invitation, age-appropriate assessments, measurable postsecondary goals, aligned course of study, Summary of Performance) and ADA/Section 504 postsecondary disclosure rules.

planningFrame.label: Support plan
planningFrame.guidance: Administer interest, study-skill, and accommodation inventories; coach Aaliyah to lead a portion of her IEP meeting; teach scripted self-advocacy role-plays; and align high school biology/health-science courses and assistive tech.

planningFrame.label: Monitoring & safeguards
planningFrame.guidance: Document formal student invitation and Prior Written Notice, track independent accommodation requests across classes each quarter, and maintain updated psychoeducational records for future college disability-office review.

successCriteria: Flags all core IDEA age-16 transition defects: failure to invite Aaliyah, absence of age-appropriate transition assessments, and vague non-measurable postsecondary goals.
Connects measurable postsecondary education and employment goals directly to high school coursework, explicit self-advocacy instruction, and nursing-relevant reading/math SDI.
Clearly explains the K-12 IDEA versus postsecondary ADA/Section 504 shift (no college IEP or FAPE; student must self-disclose, submit documentation, and request reasonable accommodations).
Specifies how a student-led IEP, accommodation portfolio, and graduation Summary of Performance (SOP) build durable adult self-determination.
commonPitfalls: Assuming Aaliyah's high school IEP transfers automatically to community college so disability counselors will arrange her audio texts without her initiating contact.
Writing a transition goal that focuses solely on high school graduation ("will pass Grade 11") rather than measurable post-high-school training and employment outcomes.
Continuing to manage Aaliyah's accommodations silently behind the scenes through Grade 12 without practicing direct self-disclosure and request scripts.
Omitting formal student invitation records, parental procedural safeguards, or transfer-of-rights notification planning prior to the age of majority.
sampleOutline: Compliance audit: At age 16, omitting Aaliyah's formal IEP invitation, age-appropriate transition assessments, and measurable postsecondary goals violates IDEA transition requirements.

Aligned transition goals: Use career/learning-profile assessments to write measurable post-graduation enrollment and CNA employment goals backed by health-science coursework, dosage-calculation math SDI, and text-to-speech mastery.
Self-advocacy curriculum: Write an annual IEP goal requiring Aaliyah to articulate her SLD strengths, barriers, and needed accommodations during teacher check-ins and a student-led IEP presentation.

Postsecondary legal bridge: Teach Aaliyah the IDEA-to-ADA/Section 504 transition (self-disclosure, documentation standards, reasonable accommodations without curriculum modification) and prepare an evidence-rich Summary of Performance before exit.
